scope: Second independent calibration sample across the real school-mock selected Year 1 Physics, AS Chemistry and Year 1 Pure Maths core flashcards; existing IDs only, no long-form exam questions.
review: Two added acceptable answers and two common incorrect answers per card. All must be verified by production evaluateCard with their exact model answers. No claim that all unseen phrasings have been checked or that every AQA bullet is covered.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What does the gradient of a displacement–time graph represent?
records.back: Velocity. A steeper gradient means greater speed; a horizontal line means v = 0. On a curve, use a tangent for instantaneous velocity.
accept: Velocity, equal to ds/dt.
Instantaneous velocity from tangent slope.
reject: Acceleration is the gradient of displacement–time graph.
Displacement is obtained from its gradient.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What do the gradient and signed area of a velocity–time graph represent?
records.back: Gradient = acceleration. Signed area under the graph = displacement.
accept: Gradient is acceleration and signed area is displacement.
Slope gives a; algebraic area gives change in position.
reject: Gradient is displacement and area is acceleration.
Area always means total distance regardless of negative velocity.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What relationship is central to the stretched-string stationary-wave practical?
accept: f=(1/(2L))*sqrt(T/mu)
Fundamental frequency is proportional to sqrt(T/μ)/2L.
reject: f=2L*sqrt(T/mu)
Frequency is proportional to the mass per length rather than inversely to its square root.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What equation links wave speed, frequency and wavelength?
accept: v=f×λ
Wave speed equals frequency multiplied by wavelength.
reject: v=f/λ
v=λ/f

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What is the separation of adjacent nodes in a stationary wave?
accept: Half a wavelength, λ/2.
Distance between neighbouring nodes is λ divided by 2.
reject: One wavelength, λ.
A quarter wavelength between adjacent nodes.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: How is refractive index related to wave speed?
accept: Refractive index n equals vacuum light speed divided by medium speed.
n=c/v.
reject: n=v/c
n=c×v

records.subject: Physics
records.front: State Snell's law for two media.
records.back: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂.
accept: n1 sin(i)=n2 sin(r)
n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂.
reject: n1 cos(i)=n2 cos(r)
n1 sin(r)=n2 sin(i) with i in medium 1.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: How do you find the magnitude of two perpendicular vector components x and y?
accept: sqrt(x^2+y^2)
Pythagoras: magnitude R=√(x²+y²).
reject: x+y is always the magnitude of the resultant.
R=√(x²−y²)

records.subject: Physics
records.front: Ignoring air resistance, what is horizontal acceleration of a projectile?
accept: Horizontal acceleration is zero.
a_x=0 in absence of air drag.
reject: Horizontal acceleration equals 9.81 m/s².
Horizontal acceleration increases during flight without resistance.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: For two series resistors, how is output p.d. found?
records.back: Vout = Vin × R₂/(R₁ + R₂), taking R₂ across the output.
accept: Vout/Vin=R2/(R1+R2) when measured across R2.
Output across the second resistor is Vin R2 divided by total series resistance.
reject: Vout=Vin×R1/(R1+R2) when measured across R2.
Output voltage always equals supply voltage in a two-resistor divider.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What is the photon-energy condition for photoelectric emission?
records.back: hf ≥ φ (photon energy at least the work function).
accept: Photon energy hf must be at least φ.
Emission requires hf≥work function.
reject: hf<φ produces photoelectron emission.
Increasing intensity makes photons below work function emit electrons.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What equation relates threshold frequency and work function?
accept: hf0=φ
Threshold frequency equals work function divided by Planck constant.
reject: hf0=φ+KEmax at threshold with positive KE.
f0=h/φ

records.subject: Physics
records.front: For stopping potential against frequency, what is the gradient?
accept: h divided by the elementary charge e.
The gradient is Planck's constant over electron charge.
reject: e/h
Gradient equals the work function φ.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: How do you calculate threshold wavelength from the work function?
records.back: λ₀ = hc/φ. Emission requires λ ≤ λ₀.
accept: Threshold wavelength λ0=hc/φ.
Maximum emission wavelength is hc divided by work function.
reject: λ0=φ/(hc)
Emission occurs only for λ>λ0.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: Why do photoelectrons have a range of kinetic energies?
records.back: Electrons can lose varying energy inside the metal before escaping; Eₖ(max) is the upper limit.
accept: Some electrons lose energy in the metal before reaching its surface.
Electrons start at different depths and may lose varying amounts of energy.
reject: All photoelectrons have identical kinetic energies.
Intensity alone determines each emitted electron's kinetic energy.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: What happens to stopping potential if light intensity doubles at fixed frequency?
records.back: It stays unchanged: photon energy and maximum photoelectron kinetic energy do not change.
accept: Stopping potential remains constant at fixed frequency.
Unchanged; max KE is independent of light intensity at the same f.
reject: Stopping potential doubles if light intensity doubles at fixed frequency.
Doubling photon count doubles photon energy.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: For a 10 kg block on a 30° slope, what is the down-slope weight component?
records.back: mg sin 30° = 10 × 9.81 × 0.5 = 49.1 N down the slope.
accept: 49.05 N down the slope.
reject: 98.1 N down the slope.
10×9.81×cos30° is the downslope component.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: On a displacement–time graph, what does a negative gradient mean?
records.back: Negative velocity: the object moves in the negative direction. A steeper slope magnitude means greater speed.
accept: Velocity is negative, i.e. movement in the negative displacement direction.
Moving towards decreasing displacement; the slope is the velocity.
reject: Negative gradient means negative acceleration.
A negative slope means the object's speed must decrease.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: A v–t graph gives +20 m and −8 m of signed area. Find displacement and distance.
accept: Displacement +12 m, total distance 28 m.
Signed areas add to 12 m; absolute areas sum to 28 m.
reject: Displacement 28 m, distance 12 m.
Both displacement and distance are 12 m.

records.subject: Physics
records.front: If velocity is negative and acceleration is negative, is the object slowing down?
records.back: No. Velocity and acceleration have the same direction, so speed increases in the negative direction.
accept: No; the object speeds up in the negative direction.
Its speed increases because v and a have the same negative sign.
reject: Yes, negative acceleration always slows a body.
The body has zero velocity because both quantities are negative.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What are the essential steps for making an accurate standard solution?
records.back: Accurately weigh, dissolve, quantitatively transfer with washings, make to the mark, stopper and invert.
accept: Weigh accurately, dissolve, rinse quantitatively into volumetric flask, make to mark, mix.
Dissolve and transfer with washings, then make up precisely and invert to mix.
reject: Fill flask to mark before transferring any measured solid.
Don't rinse beaker or funnel: the transfer is complete without washings.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What precipitate colours identify chloride, bromide and iodide after acidifying and adding AgNO₃?
records.back: AgCl white, AgBr cream, AgI yellow.
accept: Cl− white AgCl; Br− cream AgBr; I− yellow AgI.
White for chloride, cream for bromide, yellow for iodide.
reject: Cl− yellow, Br− cream, I− white.
All silver halides form identical white precipitates.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Where should the thermometer bulb be positioned during distillation?
records.back: At the entrance to the condenser/still head, so it measures vapour entering the condenser.
accept: The bulb sits by the still head at the condenser entrance.
Position it at the vapour outlet before the condenser.
reject: Thermometer bulb must be submerged in the boiling liquid.
Position the thermometer bulb inside the receiver to measure cold condensate.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Using mean bond enthalpies, how is ΔH estimated?
records.back: Σ bonds broken − Σ bonds formed.
accept: ΔH≈energy required breaking bonds minus energy released making bonds.
Sum bonds broken minus sum bonds formed.
reject: ΔH≈Σformed−Σbroken for mean bond enthalpies.
Bond formation is endothermic and bond breaking exothermic.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: How does Group 2 hydroxide solubility change down the group?
accept: Group 2 hydroxides become more soluble down the group.
Their solubility increases as you descend Group 2.
reject: Solubility of Group 2 hydroxides decreases from Mg to Ba.
All Group 2 hydroxides are equally soluble.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: How does Group 2 sulfate solubility change down the group?
accept: Sulfate solubility decreases going down Group 2.
Less soluble lower down Group 2.
reject: Group 2 sulfates become more soluble towards barium.
Barium sulfate is more soluble than magnesium sulfate.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: How does halogen oxidising power change down Group 7?
accept: Halogens become weaker oxidising agents down Group 7.
Oxidising ability declines from chlorine to bromine to iodine.
reject: Iodine is the strongest oxidising halogen.
Chlorine has lower oxidising power than iodine.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: How does halide-ion reducing power change down Group 7?
accept: Halide ions become stronger reducing agents down Group 7.
Reducing power increases from chloride to bromide to iodide.
reject: Iodide is a weaker reducing agent than chloride.
Reducing power decreases as the halide ion becomes larger.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What are the three stages of free-radical substitution?
accept: Initiation, propagation, termination.
First initiation, then propagation and finally termination.
reject: Propagation, elimination, hydrolysis.
Ionisation, acceleration and detection.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What mechanism occurs when OH⁻ reacts with a halogenoalkane to form an alcohol?
accept: Nucleophilic substitution by hydroxide ions.
OH− acts as a nucleophile replacing halide.
reject: Electrophilic addition of OH− to a halogenoalkane.
Free-radical substitution of the halo group by OH−.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Why is the C atom bonded to a halogen electrophilic?
records.back: Bond polarisation gives that carbon a partial positive charge.
accept: Because C–X is polar, carbon carries δ+.
Halogen's higher electronegativity makes attached carbon partially positive.
reject: Carbon is electrophilic because it is negatively charged.
Carbon attracts nucleophiles because carbon is δ−.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Which atom is approached by the nucleophile in substitution?
records.back: The electron-poor carbon attached to the halogen.
accept: The δ+ carbon in the carbon–halogen bond.
The carbon bonded to the leaving halogen.
reject: The electronegative halogen atom receives the nucleophile attack.
The nucleophile targets an unrelated non-electrophilic carbon by definition.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Where do C–halogen bonding electrons go during substitution?
records.back: To the departing halogen, which becomes a halide ion.
accept: The bonding electron pair goes to the leaving halogen.
Heterolytic cleavage gives the halide X− the pair.
reject: The C–X bond electrons go to the carbon and halogen leaves as X+.
Both electrons are lost into the solvent without any leaving ion.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What is the mechanistic difference between substitution and elimination?
records.back: Substitution replaces a group; elimination removes atoms/groups to create C=C.
accept: Substitution replaces a group; elimination forms a double bond by removal.
Substitution swaps atoms/groups; elimination removes HX to form an alkene.
reject: Elimination replaces the leaving halogen with OH− while substitution creates C=C.
Both mechanisms always yield an identical alcohol product.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What does m/z mean in mass spectrometry?
records.back: Mass-to-charge ratio; for a singly charged ion it matches the relative ion mass.
accept: Mass-to-charge ratio m/z.
Ion mass divided by charge number.
reject: m/z is mass multiplied by charge.
The amount of protons in the sample only.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What are the four core TOF stages in order?
records.back: Ionisation → acceleration → ion drift → detection/data analysis.
accept: Ionisation, acceleration, drift/flight, detection.
Ionise; accelerate; separate by time of flight; detect.
reject: Detection, acceleration, ionisation, flight.
Evaporation, condensation, filtration and crystallisation.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What happens to positive ions in the acceleration stage?
records.back: An electric field accelerates them, giving ions of equal charge equal kinetic energy.
accept: The electric field accelerates charged ions; equal charges at same voltage gain equal kinetic energy.
Ions are sped up by an electric potential difference, gaining qV kinetic energy.
reject: Every ion of different charge necessarily has identical kinetic energy.
Ions slow down in the acceleration region regardless of potential.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: Why is a high vacuum used in the drift tube?
records.back: To reduce collisions between moving ions and gas molecules.
accept: High vacuum prevents most collisions with background gas.
Reduce collisions with residual gas molecules.
reject: To allow frequent ion-air collisions and slow them down.
To increase the mass of ions during flight.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: How does flight time change as mass increases at fixed KE and charge?
records.back: It increases; t is proportional to the square root of mass.
accept: Flight time gets longer, scaling as square root of mass at equal energy.
The more massive ion has lower speed and takes longer; t∝√m.
reject: Heavier ions travel faster at equal kinetic energy.
Flight time is directly proportional to mass rather than its square root.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.front: What does the height/intensity of a mass spectrum peak indicate?
records.back: Relative abundance of the detected ion.
accept: Peak intensity indicates ion relative abundance.
Relative number of ions detected at that m/z.
reject: Peak height represents ion mass-to-charge instead of abundance.
The tallest peak necessarily has the largest m/z.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What is the Pythagorean trigonometric identity?
accept: sin²(x)+cos²(x)=1
Cosine squared plus sine squared equals one.
reject: sin²x−cos²x=1
sin x+cos x=1 for all x.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: For y = f(x − a), how does the graph move?
records.back: Translate a units to the right.
accept: Horizontal translation right by a (a>0).
x-coordinates increase by a for f(x−a).
reject: Translate left by a.
Reflect the graph in the y-axis.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: For y = f(x) + a, how does the graph move?
accept: Vertical translation upwards by a units.
Each y-coordinate increases by a.
reject: Vertical translation down by a units.
The graph stretches vertically by factor a.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: For a > 0, what is the horizontal scale factor of y = f(ax)?
accept: Horizontal scale factor 1/a.
All x-values are divided by a.
reject: Horizontal stretch by factor a for a>1.
Vertical stretch by scale factor a.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: How can a universal statement be disproved?
accept: One counterexample disproves a universal statement.
Find one valid case where the claim fails.
reject: A single example supporting the assertion proves it for all cases.
Checking ten true cases proves the claim always holds.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What is the nth term of an arithmetic sequence?
accept: u_n=a+(n−1)d
First term plus n minus one times common difference.
reject: u_n=a+nd

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What is the nth term of a geometric sequence?
accept: u_n=a r^(n−1)
First term multiplied by ratio to the n minus one power.
reject: u_n=a+(n−1)r
u_n=ar^n

records.subject: Maths
records.front: State the sine rule.
records.back: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C.
accept: a/sin(A)=b/sin(B)=c/sin(C)
sin A/a=sin B/b=sin C/c
reject: a/sin(B)=b/sin(A)=c/sin(C)
a cos A=b cos B=c cos C

records.subject: Maths
records.front: State the cosine rule for side a.
accept: a²=b²+c²−2bc cos A
Side a squared equals b squared plus c squared minus 2bc cos A.
reject: a²=b²+c²+2bc cos A
a²=b²+c²−2bc sin A

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What is the area formula using two sides a,b and included angle C?
accept: Area=0.5 a b sin C
One half ab times sine of the included angle.
reject: Area=ab cos C
Area=a b sin C without the half.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: Differentiate xⁿ.
accept: d/dx[x^n] = n x^(n−1)
Use power rule, multiply by n and lower exponent by one.
reject: d/dx[x^n]=n x^n
Derivative of x^n is x^(n+1)/(n+1).

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What condition identifies a stationary point?
accept: dy/dx=0
First derivative vanishes at a smooth stationary point.
reject: dy/dx is undefined at every stationary point.
The second derivative must be zero at every maximum.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: Integrate xⁿ for n≠−1.
accept: Raise the power by one then divide by the new power and add C.
reject: ∫ x^n dx = n x^(n−1)+C
Indefinite integrals never need a constant.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: How is signed area under y=f(x) from a to b found?
accept: ∫ from a to b of f(x)dx
Definite integral between a and b, keeping negative signed contributions.
reject: ∫|f(x)| dx is always the signed integral.
Area beneath the x-axis counts as positive in the signed integral.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: Magnitude of vector (a,b)?
accept: √(a²+b²)
Use Pythagoras on vector components.
reject: a+b
√(a²−b²)

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What does y = f(−x) do to the graph?
accept: Reflection in the y-axis.
Replacing x by −x mirrors horizontally across the vertical axis.
reject: Reflection in the x-axis.
Translate a units right.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What transformation maps y = f(x) to y = −f(x)?
accept: Reflect the graph in the x-axis.
Negate each y-value while leaving the x-coordinates unchanged.
reject: Reflect the graph in the y-axis.
Translate the graph to the left.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: For a>0, what does y = f(x+a) do to y = f(x)?
records.back: Translate a units to the left.
accept: Horizontal shift a units left for a>0.
Replacing x with x+a moves the graph left.
reject: Horizontal shift a units right.
Vertical shift a units upwards.

records.subject: Maths
records.front: State the binomial coefficient nCr as a factorial formula.
accept: Number of combinations n choose r equals factorial n over factorial r times factorial n−r.
reject: n!/r!

records.subject: Maths
records.front: What is the general x^r term in (a+bx)^n for a positive integer n?
accept: (n choose r)a^(n−r)(bx)^r
Binomial coefficient times a to n−r times (bx) to r.
reject: nCr×a^r×(bx)^(n−r) for the x^r term.
a^(n−r)(bx)^r without a binomial coefficient.
